title: Enterprise dedicated capacity triage: SLA tiers, GPU tiering, and scaling prioritization rubric
creator: Priya Nair
description:
Summary:
This ticket captures the intake and prioritization rubric for enterprise requests for Dedicated capacity (reserved throughput, SLA targets, GPU class guarantees, and scaling policies). The goal is to provide a repeatable triage flow that product teams and solutions engineers can use to: 1) classify incoming requests, 2) recommend an initial capacity/SLAs/GPU tier, and 3) surface contractual and engineering blockers early.

Context and motivation:
Many recent enterprise leads ask for varying combinations of: hard latency SLOs, reserved throughput guarantees, guaranteed GPU hardware classes (e.g., H100 vs A100 vs L4), and bespoke autoscaling behavior. Currently triage is ad hoc: SEs escalate to PMs and infra teams case-by-case, increasing lead time and negotiation risk. We need a lightweight rubric that balances customer requirements, runtime constraints, and Redwood’s capacity economics.

Proposed triage rubric (high level):
- Intake form fields to capture: expected QPS, peak concurrent tokens/sec, 95/99 latency targets, required GPU class, acceptable fallback model variants, burst tolerance (minutes of burst), billing commitment (monthly/annual), and regulatory constraints.
- SLA tier mapping:
  * Tier S (Critical): 95%ile latency <100ms for single-turn gen at 128 tokens; guaranteed reserved throughput (RTPU) with contractual uptime SLA 99.95%; required for financial/healthcare regulated workloads.
  * Tier A (High): 95%ile latency <250ms; RTPU preferred but burst credits allowed; uptime SLA 99.9%.
  * Tier B (Standard): best-effort latency targets, reserved throughput optional, burst-first scaling, uptime SLA 99.5%.
- GPU class decision tree:
  * If model requires >32k context / large matrix ops or customer requires top-tier latency and deterministic FP16 results => recommend H100.
  * If throughput-sensitive but cost-sensitive => A100 or mixed pool with quantized variants.
  * If cost-first or chatty low-latency workloads (embedding/semantic) => L4 or equivalent.
- Scaling policy primitives to expose to customers: minimum reserved nodes, burst credit pool, regional fallbacks, and pre-warm windows.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Reserved throughput (RTPU) vs burst credits: reserved capacity reduces variance and simplifies SLO guarantees but increases unit costs. We should recommend RTPU for Tier S and A customers with clear billing commitments. Tier B customers should default to burst credits.
- GPU guarantees increase procurement friction and can lengthen onboarding; require legal/ops signoff for H100 guarantees. Where possible, provide hardware-family guarantees with allowed substitutions and enforced latency SLAs rather than strict SKU-level promises.
- Autoscaling: we prefer continuous batching with warm caches; autoscaling should target sustained throughput rather than instantaneous QPS spikes. Provide explicit pre-warm options for onboarding windows.

Decisions made so far:
- Implement a mandatory intake form (SE/PM) capturing throughput, latency SLOs, acceptable fallbacks, and commitment level.
- Define three SLA tiers (S/A/B) as above for triage and initial pricing.
- Map hardware families instead of SKUs in contracts and require a GPU guarantee addendum for explicit SKU promises.

Open questions / engineering inputs needed:
- How to quantify RTPU units into node counts for each GPU family given variable model footprints and KV cache behavior? (ENG to provide throughput-per-node profiles per model class).
- Feasibility of offering guaranteed low-latency SLOs during global regional incidents (fallback behavior).
- Should we include a formal burst-credit marketplace (metered bursts) or just a fixed minute allocation per month?

Attachments / links:
- Intake form draft: https://drive.google.com/drive/fake-intake-draft
- Initial PRD outline: https://docs.google.com/document/fake-prd-dedicated-triage
- Engineering throughput profiles ticket: ENG-4821 (link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4821)
- Prior customer request examples: https://drive.google.com/drive/fake-customer-requests

Acceptance criteria:
- Intake form published in Confluence and linkable from SE playbook.
- Prioritization rubric doc published with SLA tier definitions and hardware-family mapping.
- Engineering runbook produced that converts RTPU units into node counts for the three canonical GPU families for small/medium/large model classes.
- SEs can produce a first-pass proposal (capacity + SLA tier + estimated monthly cost) within 3 business days of intake.

Next steps and timeline:
- Week 0 (this ticket): finalize intake fields and SLA tier definitions (owner: PM).
- Week 1: ENG to deliver throughput-per-node guidance for model classes (owner: ENG).
- Week 2: Legal to draft GPU guarantee addendum template (owner: Legal).
- Week 3: Publish SE playbook + intake flow and run a dry-run with two existing opportunities.

Acceptance / signoff requested from: Head of Solutions Engineering, Lead Runtime Engineer, Legal counsel on hardware guarantees.

Notes on risk and mitigation:
- Risk: Over-promising SKU-level guarantees -> mitigation: require ops/legal approval and prefer family-level guarantees.
- Risk: Underestimating cost impact of reserved capacity -> mitigation: show cost delta scenarios in the SE proposal template and require customer commitment level.

This ticket will be the canonical source for triaging enterprise Dedicated requests until a more automated console flow (self-serve RTPU purchase) is available.
